warmup.q: A blocking echo server gives each connection its own platform thread. 2,000 clients connect and then send nothing. How many platform threads does the server hold, and what does Thread.getState() say about them?
options: About 8, one per core, because idle sockets don't need a thread
About 2,000, each reporting WAITING, so they cost nothing
About 200, because the JVM caps platform threads at 200
warmup.why: Thread-per-connection means one thread per open socket, busy or not, and each one sits inside read(). The wait happens in native code, so getState() reports RUNNABLE. That is why a thread dump of an idle server looks busy. The demo in this lesson prints it: 2,007 platform threads for 2,000 clients, and RUNNABLE for the blocked handler.

sections.h: A blocked read holds a whole thread
sections.html:
Here is the core of every classic Java server. One thread accepts connections. Each connection gets a task that reads a line and writes it back.

Java
try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080)) {
    while (true) {
        Socket socket = server.accept();          // blocks until a client connects
        pool.execute(() -> echo(socket));         // one task per connection
    }
}

static void echo(Socket socket) {
    try (socket; var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream(), UTF_8))) {
        var out = socket.getOutputStream();
        String line;
        while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) {  // blocks until the client sends a line
            out.write((line + "\n").getBytes(UTF_8));
        }
    } catch (IOException e) {
        // the client went away
    }
}
Kotlin
ServerSocket(8080).use { server ->
    while (true) {
        val socket = server.accept()              // blocks until a client connects
        pool.execute { echo(socket) }             // one task per connection
    }
}

fun echo(socket: Socket) {
    try {
        socket.use { s ->
            val reader = s.getInputStream().bufferedReader(UTF_8)
            val out = s.getOutputStream()
            while (true) {
                val line = reader.readLine() ?: break   // blocks until the client sends a line
                out.write("$line\n".toByteArray(UTF_8))
            }
        }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        // the client went away
    }
}

The code is easy to read, and that is its strength. The cost hides in readLine().

Go one level down to see it. A socket is the kernel's object for one end of a TCP connection, and the kernel keeps a receive buffer for it: bytes that have arrived from the network but that your program hasn't read yet. read() copies bytes out of that buffer. If the buffer is empty, the kernel takes the calling thread off the CPU and parks it on the socket's wait list. When a packet arrives, the kernel appends its bytes to the buffer and wakes the parked thread, which then returns from read(). While the client thinks, or sits idle on a keep-alive connection (one it leaves open between requests), that thread can do nothing else.

Two things surprise people the first time they look.

The thread is not free to keep. A Java platform thread is a thin wrapper around one operating system thread, with its own stack, and Jetty's documentation puts it at about 1 MiB of native memory. The OS scheduler also has to track every one of them.

And a thread dump hides the waiting. A platform thread blocked in a socket read reports RUNNABLE, because the JVM sees it running native code (SocketDispatcher.read0). A server with 2,000 idle connections shows 2,000 runnable threads and almost no CPU use.

Vert.x's documentation makes the same point about every blocking API: while the thread waits for a result it can do nothing else, so a lot of concurrency needs a lot of threads. For a blocking server, the question is never how fast one request runs. It is how many threads you can hold, and how many your traffic needs.

try.title: Count the threads
steps: Open ThreadPerConnectionDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin, ThreadPerConnectionDemo.kt). It connects 2,000 clients that never send anything: first to a server with a cached thread pool, then to one with a virtual thread per connection.
Before you run it, write down two predictions: how many platform threads the first server holds, and what getState() returns for a handler stuck in read().
Run it from labs/ with the command below. Then run it again with -Pargs=5000 added.

code.title: ThreadPerConnectionDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l01; import java.io.IOException; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.ServerSocket; import java.net.Socket; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * Opens N idle connections to a blocking server and counts what they cost. * Args: [clients, default 2000] [seconds to hold the connections open, default 0] */ public class ThreadPerConnectionDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int clients = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 2_000; int holdSeconds = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 0; run("platform thread per connection", Executors.newCachedThreadPool(), clients, holdSeconds); run("virtual thread per connection", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), clients, holdSeconds); } static void run(String label, ExecutorService handlers, int clients, int holdSeconds) throws Exception { ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); // counts platform threads only int before = mx.getThreadCount(); List<Thread> handlerThreads = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(0, clients, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress())) { Thread acceptor = new Thread(() -> { try { while (true) { Socket s = server.accept(); handlers.execute(() -> { handlerThreads.add(Thread.currentThread()); try (s) { s.getInputStream().read(); // blocks until the client sends a byte or closes } catch (IOException ignored) { } }); } } catch (IOException serverClosed) { } }, "acceptor"); acceptor.setDaemon(true); acceptor.start(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<Socket> open = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < clients; i++) open.add(new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), server.getLocalPort())); while (handlerThreads.size() < clients) Thread.sleep(10); System.out.printf("%s: %,d idle clients connected in %,d ms%n", label, clients, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); System.out.printf(" platform threads: %d before, %d now%n", before, mx.getThreadCount()); System.out.printf(" a handler blocked in read() reports state %s%n", handlerThreads.get(0).getState()); if (holdSeconds > 0) { System.out.printf(" holding the connections for %d s (pid %d)%n", holdSeconds, ProcessHandle.current().pid()); Thread.sleep(holdSeconds * 1_000L); } for (Socket s : open) s.close(); } handlers.shutdown(); handlers.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

alt.title: ThreadPerConnectionDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.nio.l01 import java.io.IOException import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.net.InetAddress import java.net.ServerSocket import java.net.Socket import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** * Opens N idle connections to a blocking server and counts what they cost. * Args: [clients, default 2000] [seconds to hold the connections open, default 0] */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val clients = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 2_000 val holdSeconds = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 0 runIdleClients("platform thread per connection", Executors.newCachedThreadPool(), clients, holdSeconds) runIdleClients("virtual thread per connection", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), clients, holdSeconds) } private fun runIdleClients(label: String, handlers: ExecutorService, clients: Int, holdSeconds: Int) { val mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() // counts platform threads only val before = mx.threadCount val handlerThreads = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Thread>() ServerSocket(0, clients, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress()).use { server -> thread(isDaemon = true, name = "acceptor") { try { while (true) { val s = server.accept() handlers.execute { handlerThreads += Thread.currentThread() try { s.use { it.getInputStream().read() } // blocks until the client sends a byte or closes } catch (_: IOException) { } } } } catch (_: IOException) { // server closed } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() val open = List(clients) { Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), server.localPort) } while (handlerThreads.size < clients) Thread.sleep(10) println("%s: %,d idle clients connected in %,d ms".format(label, clients, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) println(" platform threads: $before before, ${mx.threadCount} now") println(" a handler blocked in read() reports state ${handlerThreads.first().state}") if (holdSeconds > 0) { println(" holding the connections for $holdSeconds s (pid ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()})") Thread.sleep(holdSeconds * 1_000L) } open.forEach { it.close() } } handlers.shutdown() handlers.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) }

try.expect: On my 4-core machine with JDK 21 the platform version went from 6 platform threads to 2,007, one per client plus the JVM's own, and the blocked handler reported RUNNABLE. The virtual version held the same 2,000 connections with 15 platform threads, and its blocked handler reported WAITING. With 5,000 clients the first number became 5,007 and the second stayed at 15.

sections.h: Little's law counts the threads you need
sections.html:
You met Little's law in the executors and virtual threads tracks. The number of requests in a system equals the arrival rate times the time each one spends there: L = λ × W. With thread-per-request, L is also the number of threads you need.

Take an authorization service. At peak it gets 800 requests a second. Each request spends 30 ms in your code and 120 ms waiting for the card issuer. That is 800 × 0.15 s = 120 requests in flight, so 120 busy threads, and a pool of 200 copes. If the issuer slows to 600 ms, the same traffic needs 800 × 0.63 s = 504 threads. Your CPU is no busier. The extra threads are all waiting.

Thread-per-connection is worse than thread-per-request, because it pays for connections, not requests. A connection holds its thread for its whole life, including the idle time between requests. Picture 10,000 point-of-sale terminals that each keep a connection open and send one request every 10 seconds. That is 1,000 requests a second. At 150 ms each, Little's law says 150 are in flight. The thread-per-connection server still needs 10,000 threads, because 9,850 of them sit in read() waiting for their terminal's next request.

That gap explains two defaults you may have seen in Tomcat's connector docs. maxThreads is 200 and caps simultaneous requests. maxConnections is 8,192 and caps open connections. The NIO connector's poller watches the idle sockets with select(), so a worker thread is needed only while a request is being processed. Threads follow requests in flight, not open sockets.

Each extra platform thread costs a stack and a slot in the scheduler. When many threads are runnable, the OS also pays for context switches: saving one thread's registers and loading another's, with the CPU caches going cold in between. A few thousand works, as the demo showed. Tens of thousands is where servers in the late 1990s fell over, and it is still a bad place to be.

try.title: Do the arithmetic before the incident
steps: A settlement service reads from Kafka and calls a ledger API: 300 calls a second, 40 ms in your own code, 260 ms waiting for the ledger. How many threads does thread-per-request need?
The ledger has an incident and takes 2 s per call. Traffic stays the same. How many threads now?
Open the lab test fixedPoolCapsConnections. Which of your two numbers would a fixed pool of 100 survive, and what would callers see in the other case?
try.expect: 300 × 0.3 s = 90 threads normally, and 300 × 2.04 s = 612 threads during the incident. A pool of 100 copes with the first. In the second, tasks queue behind busy threads, latency climbs past every client timeout, and the service looks down while its CPU is idle. The pool ran out of threads that were waiting, not threads that were working.

sections.h: C10K: ten thousand clients at once
sections.html:
In 1999 Dan Kegel wrote a page called "The C10K problem". The name is short for ten thousand concurrent clients. His argument was that the hardware of the day could already serve that many connections and the server software could not, because of how it used threads and system calls.

The answer the industry settled on is the one this whole track is about: stop giving each connection a thread. Put many sockets in non-blocking mode, where a read on an empty receive buffer returns 0 bytes at once instead of parking the thread. Then ask the kernel one question: which of these sockets are ready right now? select and poll were the first system calls for that, and they take the whole list of sockets on every call, which gets slow with thousands of them. Linux added epoll and the BSDs and macOS added kqueue. Both keep the watched sockets inside the kernel and report only the ones that are ready. One thread can then watch thousands of connections and run code only for those with data. That loop (wait for ready sockets, serve each one a little, wait again) is called an event loop.

That one idea has many names on the JVM:

  • java.nio's Selector, which is epoll on Linux and kqueue on macOS (lesson 2).
  • Netty's event loop: one thread running a selector and your handlers (lessons 3 and 4).
  • Vert.x and Quarkus, which run on Netty (lessons 5 and 6).
  • Jetty's ManagedSelector (lesson 7).
  • The JDK's internal poller, which virtual threads use when they block on a socket (lesson 8).

The price is the programming model. A thread that serves thousands of sockets must never block on any one of them. Every read has to return at once with whatever bytes are there, maybe none. Every write has to accept that only part of the buffer went out. Your code becomes a small state machine per connection, called whenever the kernel reports that something happened. The rest of this track is about writing that state machine well, or picking a framework that writes it for you.

try.title: See the waiting threads in a dump
steps: Start the demo with 300 clients and hold the connections for 20 seconds: run the command below.

While it holds the platform-thread version, run jcmd workbench.nio.l01.ThreadPerConnectionDemo Thread.print | grep -c NioSocketImpl.implRead in a second terminal. jcmd accepts the main class name instead of a pid.
Run the same jcmd line again once the demo prints the virtual-thread section. Predict the count first.
try.expect: The first count is 300: each handler's stack runs through NioSocketImpl.implRead down to SocketDispatcher.read0, and its state line says RUNNABLE. The second count is 0. Thread.print lists platform threads only, and the 300 virtual threads are parked off any thread. Lesson 8 shows how to find them.

sections.h: Two ways out: fewer threads, or cheaper threads
sections.html:
There are two ways to serve 10,000 connections from one JVM.

The first is the C10K answer: a few threads, each running an event loop over many non-blocking sockets. Netty, Vert.x and Quarkus work this way. It scales very far, and you pay with code that must never block. Call JDBC from an event loop and every other connection on that loop stops until the query returns.

The second arrived in JDK 21: virtual threads (JEP 444). You keep the blocking code from the first section and change the executor.

Java
// echo() stays exactly as it was
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
Kotlin
// echo() stays exactly as it was
val pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()

The demo showed the effect: 2,000 blocked readers on 15 platform threads. It works because the JDK runs an event loop for you. When a virtual thread's socket read would block, the JDK registers the socket with an internal poller built on epoll or kqueue, parks the virtual thread, and frees its carrier (the platform thread that was running it) for other work. Lesson 8 opens that poller up.

Neither way makes a single request faster. Non-blocking IO and virtual threads buy concurrency per unit of memory, not latency. A request that waits 120 ms for the card issuer still takes 120 ms. Neither removes the limits behind your service either. If 10,000 virtual threads all want one of 20 database connections, 9,980 of them wait in the pool's queue. The virtual threads track shows how to cap that with a semaphore.

My default for a new blocking service is virtual threads. I'd move to an event-loop framework when measurements say memory per connection or scheduling is the problem, or when the service already lives on one, as every Quarkus service does. Most payment services hit the limits of their downstreams long before either wall.

try.title: Swap the executor, keep the code
steps: Finish the lab first, so BlockingEchoServer works.
Read the test virtualThreadsScale. It passes Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() to the same server class that idleClientsHoldThreads runs on a cached pool.
Change its client count from 500 to 2,000 and run only that test with --tests '*virtualThreadsScale'. Predict whether the platform-thread assertion still holds.
try.expect: It still passes. The platform-thread count grows by a few threads (carriers and poller threads) whether 500 or 2,000 connections are open, because a parked virtual thread holds no OS thread. Put the count back to 500 when you're done.

analogy: A thread-per-connection server is a restaurant that gives every table its own waiter for the whole evening. The waiter stands by the table while the guests read the menu, eat and talk, and serves nobody else. Forty tables need forty waiters even when only three tables want something. An event loop is one waiter walking the room who stops only at tables where someone raised a hand. The analogy breaks at the kernel: a real waiter has to scan the room, while epoll hands the event loop a list of exactly the tables with raised hands.
world: Your Quarkus services already avoid thread-per-connection: Vert.x accepts and reads every connection on a few event-loop threads and borrows a worker thread only while a blocking endpoint runs. Thread-per-connection still hides in the code around them: a TCP client to a card network that keeps one reader thread per terminal, an ISO 8583 gateway written years ago, or a Kafka consumer you scaled by adding threads that each block on a 120 ms issuer call. Run Little's law on each one: requests per second times seconds per request gives threads in flight. Then compare that with the threads it actually holds while it waits.
mistake: The common mistake is sizing a blocking server by CPU: "we have 8 cores, so 16 threads is plenty." That rule is for CPU-bound work. A thread waiting on a socket uses no CPU, so the number comes from Little's law, and for thread-per-connection from the number of open sockets. The opposite mistake usually follows the first outage: raising maxThreads to 5,000 to ride out a slow downstream. Now a slow issuer fills 5,000 threads instead of 200, memory climbs, and the issuer receives 5,000 concurrent calls it can't serve either. Size from the traffic you expect, cap concurrency toward each dependency, and make idle connections cheap with an event loop or virtual threads.

compare.title: One virtual thread per connection, in both languages

java.title: VirtualEchoServer.java
java.html: try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { while (true) { Socket socket = server.accept(); pool.submit(() -> echo(socket)); // a blocked read parks the virtual thread } }

kotlin.title: VirtualEchoServer.kt
kotlin.html: ServerSocket(8080).use { server -> Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { pool -> while (true) { val socket = server.accept() pool.submit { echo(socket) } // a blocked read parks the virtual thread } } }

compare.note: The JDK does the work in both: ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since JDK 19, so Java's try-with-resources and Kotlin's use both shut the pool down and wait for running tasks. The difference worth knowing is coroutines. A Kotlin coroutine that calls the blocking readLine() does not suspend. It holds its dispatcher thread for the whole wait, so launch(Dispatchers.IO) { echo(socket) } is thread-per-connection again, capped by the IO dispatcher's 64 threads. Coroutines only free the thread when the IO call itself suspends, which is what Ktor and Vert.x's Kotlin APIs provide.

worked.title: Size a terminal gateway with Little's law

steps.say: A gateway keeps one TCP connection per payment terminal: 6,000 terminals. Each terminal sends an authorization every 20 seconds. The gateway spends 15 ms of CPU and 135 ms waiting for the card switch per request. Today it runs one platform thread per connection.
steps.code: // 1. today: one platform thread per terminal connection ExecutorService pool = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); while (true) { Socket terminal = server.accept(); pool.execute(() -> serveTerminal(terminal)); // loops: read request, call switch, reply }

alt.html: // 1. today: one platform thread per terminal connection val pool = Executors.newCachedThreadPool() while (true) { val terminal = server.accept() pool.execute { serveTerminal(terminal) } // loops: read request, call switch, reply }

steps.say: Apply Little's law to requests, then compare with connections. The gap is the cost of idle connections.
steps.code:
arrival rate   = 6,000 terminals / 20 s       = 300 requests/s
time in system = 15 ms + 135 ms              = 0.15 s
in flight      = 300 x 0.15                  = 45 requests
threads held   = one per connection          = 6,000 threads
idle threads   = 6,000 - 45                  = 5,955 waiting in read()

steps.say: Make idle connections cheap. A virtual thread parked in read() holds no OS thread, so the 5,955 idle connections cost a little heap each instead of a platform thread each. The serving code does not change.
steps.code: // 2. same serveTerminal(), cheap waiting ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();

alt.html: // 2. same serveTerminal(), cheap waiting val pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()

steps.say: Now protect the switch. It allows 64 concurrent requests. The old design limited concurrency by accident, through thread count. Virtual threads remove that accident, so put the limit back on purpose, around the call that needs it.
steps.code: // 3. cap concurrency toward the switch, not the number of connections private final Semaphore switchSlots = new Semaphore(64); AuthResponse authorize(AuthRequest req) throws InterruptedException { switchSlots.acquire(); try { return cardSwitch.send(req); // 135 ms } finally { switchSlots.release(); } }

alt.html: // 3. cap concurrency toward the switch, not the number of connections private val switchSlots = Semaphore(64) fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): AuthResponse { switchSlots.acquire() try { return cardSwitch.send(req) // 135 ms } finally { switchSlots.release() } }

lab.title: Watch a blocking server run out of threads
steps: Run the tests once. All four fail: the accept loop and the handler are stubs, so the clients time out after 3 seconds.
Write acceptLoop(): while the server socket is open, accept() a socket, add it to open, and call handlers.execute(() -> handle(socket)). Return when accept() throws.

Write handle(Socket): increment inHandler, wrap the input stream in a UTF-8 BufferedReader, and write every line back with \n and a flush(). In finally, remove the socket from open and decrement inHandler.
Run the tests until all four pass. Then read fixedPoolCapsConnections and virtualThreadsScale side by side: the same server code with three executors gives three very different limits.
hints: try (socket; BufferedReader in = ...) closes the socket for you. Since Java 9 you can list an existing effectively final variable in try-with-resources.
accept() throws a SocketException once close() closes the server socket. Treat that as the signal to return.
After shutdownNow(), execute throws RejectedExecutionException. Catch it in the accept loop too, so the acceptor thread ends quietly.

drill.title: Write a thread-per-connection echo server from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write static void serve(ServerSocket server, ExecutorService pool) that accepts forever and echoes each line back on its own task. Then answer: with Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10), what does the 11th idle client see when it sends a line?

answer.html: static void serve(ServerSocket server, ExecutorService pool) throws IOException { while (true) { Socket socket = server.accept(); pool.execute(() -> { try (socket; var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream(), UTF_8))) { var out = socket.getOutputStream(); String line; while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) { out.write((line + "\n").getBytes(UTF_8)); out.flush(); } } catch (IOException ignored) { } }); } } // The 11th client connects fine: the acceptor accepts it and queues its task. // Nobody reads its line until one of the first 10 clients disconnects.

alt.html: fun serve(server: ServerSocket, pool: ExecutorService) { while (true) { val socket = server.accept() pool.execute { try { socket.use { s -> val reader = s.getInputStream().bufferedReader(UTF_8) val out = s.getOutputStream() while (true) { val line = reader.readLine() ?: break out.write("$line\n".toByteArray(UTF_8)) out.flush() } } } catch (_: IOException) { } } } } // The 11th client connects fine: the acceptor accepts it and queues its task. // Nobody reads its line until one of the first 10 clients disconnects.

recap: A blocking read holds its thread for the whole wait. A platform thread blocked in a socket read even reports RUNNABLE.
Little's law, L = λ × W, gives the requests in flight. Thread-per-request needs that many threads; thread-per-connection needs one per open socket, idle or not.
The C10K problem (Dan Kegel, 1999) is serving ten thousand concurrent clients. Thread-per-connection didn't get there.
The fix was readiness notification: non-blocking sockets plus select, poll, and later epoll or kqueue, so one thread watches thousands of sockets.
Virtual threads keep blocking code and let the JDK's poller do the watching. Neither they nor event loops make one request faster, and neither removes downstream limits.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to raise maxThreads from 200 to 4,000 because the card issuer got slow and requests piled up. Explain what those threads were doing, what Little's law says about the incident, and what you would do instead.
explain.answer: The threads were not working, they were waiting: each one sat in a blocking call to the issuer. Little's law says in-flight requests equal arrival rate times latency, so when the issuer's latency went up the same traffic needed many more threads, and the pool ran out. Raising the limit to 4,000 makes waiting more expensive and sends 4,000 concurrent calls to an issuer that is already struggling. I would keep the pool sized for normal traffic, cap concurrency toward the issuer with a semaphore or bulkhead, add a timeout so callers fail fast, and, if the problem is the cost of waiting threads, move the blocking code to virtual threads or an event loop so waiting stops costing an OS thread.

deeper.html:
"About 1 MiB per platform thread" needs one detail to be useful. On 64-bit Linux the default stack size (-Xss) is 1 MB, and the JVM reserves that much address space per thread. The kernel commits pages only as the stack actually grows, so 2,000 idle threads don't use 2 GB of RAM. They do use real memory for the pages they touched, kernel structures per thread, and a scheduler entry each.

You can see the JVM's view with Native Memory Tracking. Start a JVM with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary. The Thread section shows how many threads exist and their reserved and committed stack memory. Run it on the demo while it holds 2,000 platform threads and again during the virtual-thread phase.

The limit you hit first in production is often not memory. Containers and hosts cap the number of processes and threads per user or per cgroup (ulimit -u, the cgroup pids.max). When a JVM can't create a thread it throws OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread, a confusing name for a thread-count limit.

Thread-per-connection is not always wrong. An internal service with 50 long-lived connections and steady traffic is simpler and faster to debug with one thread per connection, and the thread count never gets near any limit. The problem starts when connection count grows independently of the work, as with keep-alive clients, terminals and mobile apps.
